title: Automating Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) Formulation Generation from Natural Language
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on AI as a Tool for Mathematics, Computer Science, and Machine Learning (AI4Research)
summary: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) is a central formulation for combinatorial optimization and has gained increasing attention due to its compatibility with quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and quantum-inspired solvers. However, translating natural-language problem descriptions into correct QUBO formulations remains difficult, requiring the identification of binary variables, constraints, objective functions, penalty terms, and suitable penalty weights. This process is time-consuming and often demands substantial domain expertise. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end multi-agent framework that automatically generates QUBO formulations from natural-language problem descriptions, supported by structured or unstructured test cases. To evaluate its performance, We also introduce QUBOBench, a benchmark containing 100 combinatorial optimization problems across 12 application domains, curated from peer-reviewed literature, competitions, and canonical NP-hard problems. Experimental results show that our framework achieves 68% accuracy on QUBOBench, outperforming a direct single-call baseline by 22%. Further analysis identifies iterative self-repair as the most important component contributing to improved performance. The data and code are open-sourced at https://quitttcat.github.io/QuantumQUBOAgent.

AI.tldr: An AI framework that automatically generates QUBO formulations from natural language descriptions, achieving 68% accuracy on a new benchmark of 100 combinatorial optimization problems.
AI.motivation: Translating natural-language problem descriptions into correct Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations is difficult, time-consuming, and requires substantial domain expertise, creating a barrier to using quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and quantum-inspired solvers.
AI.method: An end-to-end multi-agent framework that automatically generates QUBO formulations from natural-language problem descriptions, supported by structured or unstructured test cases. The framework includes iterative self-repair mechanisms.
AI.result: The framework achieves 68% accuracy on QUBOBench (100 combinatorial optimization problems across 12 domains), outperforming a direct single-call baseline by 22%. Iterative self-repair is identified as the most important component for improved performance.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent framework successfully automates QUBO formulation generation from natural language, making quantum optimization more accessible. The open-sourced QUBOBench provides a valuable benchmark for future research in this area.

title: Byzantine-Robust Federated Fire Detection with a Rotating Coordinator
summary: We study the application of federated learning (FL) to indoor fire detection. Such fire-detection systems use edge cameras that record sensitive footage which cannot easily be collected at a central server. Existing federated solutions leave three practical obstacles unaddressed: limited uplink bandwidth, Byzantine (malicious or faulty) clients, and unconditional trust in a single, permanently fixed aggregation server. Our main contributions address all three. In particular, we provide (i) a curated indoor fire-detection dataset assembled from eight public sources; (ii) an edge-deployable detector whose model updates are compressed up to 10 time with only a small loss in balanced accuracy; and (iii) a semi-decentralized Byzantine-robust FL method that combines history-aware aggregation with a rotating coordinator, evicting stealthy attacks that per-round filters miss while removing the fixed-server single point of failure. On the held-out test set the rotating-coordinator method matches its fixed-server counterpart in accuracy and detection speed, and a physically distributed six-node cloud deployment confirms feasibility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Byzantine-robust federated learning system for indoor fire detection using edge cameras, addressing bandwidth constraints, malicious clients, and single-point server failures through model compression and rotating coordinator aggregation.
AI.motivation: Indoor fire detection systems use edge cameras that capture sensitive footage which cannot be centrally collected due to privacy/bandwidth concerns. Existing federated learning approaches don't address three key practical obstacles: limited uplink bandwidth, Byzantine (malicious/faulty) clients, and unconditional trust in a single, permanently fixed aggregation server.
AI.method: Three main contributions: (1) A curated indoor fire-detection dataset from eight public sources, (2) An edge-deployable detector with model updates compressed up to 10x with minimal accuracy loss, and (3) A semi-decentralized Byzantine-robust FL method combining history-aware aggregation with a rotating coordinator to detect stealthy attacks and eliminate fixed-server single point of failure.
AI.result: The rotating-coordinator method matches its fixed-server counterpart in accuracy and detection speed on held-out test set. A physically distributed six-node cloud deployment confirms the feasibility of the approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed federated learning system effectively addresses the three practical obstacles in indoor fire detection, providing a robust, privacy-preserving solution with compressed communications, Byzantine robustness, and distributed coordination that eliminates single points of failure.

title: GEOSTEER: Geodesic Optimization for Activation Steering in Large Language Models
summary: Activation steering provides a lightweight way to control large language models (LLMs) by modifying their hidden activations at inference time. Among these approaches, norm-preserving steering aims to change model behavior without altering the activation norm, reducing the risk of representation collapse and degradation. However, existing norm-preserving methods are limited by predefined steering trajectories and by their reliance on one-step updates, which may fail to capture the complex structure of activation distributions. We propose GeoSteer, an optimization-based method for norm-preserving activation steering. GeoSteer formulates steering as a Riemannian optimization problem and updates activations through a sequence of small geodesic steps on the representation manifold. To avoid fixed steering directions, GeoSteer learns a nonlinear activation-space objective that distinguishes desired from undesired activations, and uses this function to adaptively guide each steering step. This multistep formulation yields smoother, more stable, and more consistent steering behavior while preserving the activation norm. Across TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts, and UltraFeedback benchmarks, GeoSteer consistently improves over state-of-the-art activation steering baselines. These results suggest that norm-preserving steering can be made more effective by replacing predefined one-step edits with adaptive, geometry-aware optimization.

AI.tldr: GeoSteer is a Riemannian optimization method for norm-preserving activation steering in LLMs that uses multi-step geodesic updates on the representation manifold with learned nonlinear objectives, outperforming existing one-step methods across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing norm-preserving steering methods are limited by: 1) predefined steering trajectories, 2) reliance on one-step updates that fail to capture complex activation distributions, and 3) potential for representation collapse if activation norms are not preserved.
AI.method: GeoSteer formulates steering as a Riemannian optimization problem on the representation manifold. It uses multi-step geodesic updates guided by a learned nonlinear objective function that distinguishes desired from undesired activations, enabling adaptive steering while preserving activation norms.
AI.result: Across TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts, and UltraFeedback benchmarks, GeoSteer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art activation steering baselines, demonstrating smoother, more stable, and more consistent steering behavior.
AI.conclusion: Norm-preserving activation steering can be significantly improved by replacing predefined one-step edits with adaptive, geometry-aware Riemannian optimization that better captures activation distribution structure while maintaining representation quality.

title: Benchmark Radar: A Living Database and Search Engine for AI Benchmarks and Evaluation
comment: Project site: https://benchmark-radar.org/ Code: https://github.com/ktwu01/benchmark-radar
summary: Benchmark researchers and developers of large language models (LLMs) and other AI systems need to find relevant evaluations, locate their benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores. We present Benchmark Radar, a living database and search engine for retrieval and discovery of AI benchmarks, covering LLM evaluation, agentic and tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. The system combines daily discovery of benchmark papers, repositories, datasets, and releases with a searchable benchmark catalog, mentions in model cards and technical reports, and score histories. It retains source identities and citations so readers can inspect candidate benchmarks and their evaluation evidence. Daily discovery draws on 37 sources: 13 direct connectors and 24 first-party research and engineering feeds. The catalog contains 1,283 source records drawn from 4 benchmark catalogs and 12,916 numeric observations on 790 records. We describe collection and retrieval, audit the full catalog, and examine benchmark saturation, adoption trends, and the limits of score comparisons. A worked example walks through a complete prior-art search, showing how to query the catalog and inspect benchmark evidence when designing a new evaluation. We release the web dashboard with a benchmark leaderboard, a Pareto frontier view of score against measured use, saturation and trend views, daily feeds, downloadable evidence, a command-line interface (CLI) for offline queries, and reproducible analysis.

AI.tldr: Benchmark Radar is a living database and search engine for AI benchmarks that helps researchers discover, understand, and compare evaluation metrics for LLMs and AI systems through automated collection, searchable catalog, and analysis tools.
AI.motivation: Researchers and developers of AI systems struggle to find relevant evaluations, locate benchmark datasets and code, and understand the settings behind reported scores, creating a need for organized benchmark discovery and comparison tools.
AI.method: Daily discovery from 37 sources (13 direct connectors and 24 first-party feeds) combined with a searchable catalog containing 1,283 source records and 12,916 numeric observations. The system maintains source identities, citations, and provides various interfaces including web dashboard, CLI, and downloadable evidence.
AI.result: Created a comprehensive benchmark discovery system covering LLM evaluation, agentic/tool-use benchmarks, coding, reasoning, safety, and domain-specific evaluations. Includes 790 records with numeric observations, and provides tools for prior-art search, leaderboards, Pareto frontiers, trend analysis, and reproducible research.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark Radar addresses the critical need for organized benchmark discovery and comparison in AI research, enabling better evaluation design through comprehensive search, evidence inspection, and trend analysis, while providing practical tools for the research community.

title: Learning Orthogonal Multi-Index Models Beyond Small Initialization: Incremental Learning, Competitive Dynamics and Symmetry
comment: 102 pages
summary: Recent work has identified incremental learning in shallow networks trained on single-index and multi-index models. However, existing analyses often rely on simplifying settings, such as small initialization, correlation loss, or layer-wise training. These choices reduce neuron interactions and leave some feature learning dynamics under standard initialization unexplored. We study training dynamics for polynomial-width two-layer networks learning orthogonal multi-index targets under standard initialization using polynomially many samples. We first prove that incremental learning still occurs: the loss decreases sequentially according to the Hermite expansion of the target, with lower-order components learned before higher-order components recover the individual target directions. In this standard initialization regime, training also shows a competitive reallocation of parameter mass: after the total mass fits the target mean and stabilizes, mass shifts into the target subspace and then concentrates on aligned neurons. Our theoretical analysis uses slightly modified gradient flow, while vanilla gradient descent empirically exhibits the same qualitative dynamics. Technically, we introduce a symmetry-based finite-width approximation via symmetrized networks, rather than comparing directly with an infinite-width limit. This yields better control of approximation errors and may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that incremental learning occurs in polynomial-width two-layer networks trained with standard initialization on orthogonal multi-index targets, with loss decreasing sequentially according to Hermite expansion order, and reveals competitive parameter mass reallocation dynamics.
AI.motivation: Previous analyses of incremental learning in shallow networks often rely on simplifying settings like small initialization, correlation loss, or layer-wise training, which reduce neuron interactions and leave feature learning dynamics under standard initialization unexplored.
AI.method: The authors study training dynamics for polynomial-width two-layer networks learning orthogonal multi-index targets under standard initialization using polynomially many samples. They use a symmetry-based finite-width approximation via symmetrized networks instead of comparing directly with infinite-width limits.
AI.result: 1) Incremental learning still occurs: loss decreases sequentially according to Hermite expansion of the target, with lower-order components learned before higher-order components. 2) Competitive parameter mass reallocation: after total mass fits target mean and stabilizes, mass shifts into target subspace and concentrates on aligned neurons.
AI.conclusion: The theoretical analysis reveals that incremental learning persists under standard initialization regimes, and the symmetry-based finite-width approximation approach provides better control of approximation errors and may be of independent technical interest.

title: KuaiRP Series Role-playing Models Technical Report
summary: This paper introduces the complete technical solution for the KuaiRP series of role-playing models. We aim to achieve four core objectives for a dedicated role-playing model: simplified prompt engineering, highly stable output quality, built-in domain world knowledge, and high-efficiency deployment with a small parameter size. However, effectively injecting deep domain knowledge often leads to a severe catastrophic forgetting of the model's general agent capabilities. To overcome this trade-off, we propose a multi-stage training pipeline. First, we design a standardized character template and construct an SFT data pipeline based on user behavior simulation and reverse profile filtering. Next, we utilize a rule-based composite reward function during the Reinforcement Learning (RL) phase to eliminate common degradation phenomena like length expansion and repetitive generation. Finally, to recover the general capabilities compromised during SFT and RL, we propose a novel self-distillation paradigm using Two-stage On-Policy Distillation (OPD) equipped with Cumulative-Divergence Decay (CDD). By using the domain-adapted model as the teacher and the original base model as the student, we effectively balance deep domain knowledge injection with the preservation of general agent capabilities. Experimental results demonstrate that the KuaiRP models not only match the current state-of-the-art proprietary models in role-playing fidelity within our target domains, but also successfully recover general agent capabilities, maintaining extremely low deployment costs.

AI.tldr: KuaiRP introduces a role-playing model with multi-stage training that overcomes catastrophic forgetting when injecting domain knowledge while maintaining general capabilities and low deployment costs.
AI.motivation: There's a trade-off between effectively injecting deep domain knowledge into role-playing models and maintaining their general agent capabilities, often leading to catastrophic forgetting of those general capabilities.
AI.method: A multi-stage training pipeline: 1) Design standardized character template with SFT data pipeline using user behavior simulation and reverse profile filtering, 2) Reinforcement Learning with rule-based composite reward function to eliminate issues like length expansion and repetitive generation, 3) Novel self-distillation using Two-stage On-Policy Distillation with Cumulative-Divergence Decay to recover general capabilities compromised during SFT and RL.
AI.result: KuaiRP models match state-of-the-art proprietary models in role-playing fidelity within target domains while successfully recovering general agent capabilities and maintaining extremely low deployment costs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-stage training pipeline effectively balances deep domain knowledge injection with preservation of general agent capabilities, achieving both high role-playing fidelity and low deployment costs.

title: Same Day, Same Story; One Day Ahead, a Different Signal: The Dual Validity of Financial Sentiment
summary: Financial NLP has a standard workflow: validate a sentiment tool against human labels, then trust it to extract market signal. This assumes the two evaluations measure the same thing. We test that assumption in a setting where both can be measured at once: a corpus of securities class actions (2002-2025) linking 70,500 X messages to abnormal stock returns, with a single-annotator human labelled gold sample. Running five instruments (VADER, Loughran-McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through one identical pipeline, we find that the relationship between construct and predictive validity depends on the sampling convention and score representation. Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. On a fixed-n panel, however, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, while the coarse ordering remains weak. Benchmark agreement therefore establishes semantic validity but does not by itself determine predictive rankings. In a conversation that is 17.6% spam, message volume predicts neither market damage nor settlement size.

AI.tldr: Financial sentiment analysis tools' agreement with human labels doesn't necessarily predict their ability to forecast stock market movements, as shown in securities class action cases.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the standard assumption in financial NLP that sentiment tools validated against human labels can automatically extract reliable market signals. The researchers question whether construct validity (agreement with humans) and predictive validity (forecasting market movements) measure the same thing.
AI.method: The study uses a corpus of securities class actions (2002-2025) linking 70,500 X (Twitter) messages to abnormal stock returns. They employ a single-annotator human-labeled gold sample and test five sentiment instruments (VADER, Loughran-McDonald, FinBERT, Twitter-RoBERTa, and an LLM annotator) through identical pipelines. They examine the relationship between construct and predictive validity under different sampling conventions (method-specific vs. fixed-n panel) and score representations.
AI.result: Under conventional method-specific sampling, human agreement aligns more closely with graded same-day associations than with one-day leads. On a fixed-n panel, agreement has similar graded rank correlations at both horizons, but coarse ordering remains weak. Sentiment tools' agreement with human labels establishes semantic validity but doesn't determine predictive rankings. Additionally, in a dataset with 17.6% spam, message volume doesn't predict market damage or settlement size.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark agreement (construct validity) establishes semantic validity of sentiment tools but doesn't by itself determine predictive validity rankings for market forecasting. The relationship between the two types of validity depends on sampling conventions and score representations, challenging the standard workflow assumption in financial NLP.

title: Measuring the Value of World-Model Updates: A Counterfactual Utility Protocol for Continual Adaptation
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, under review at the CWM workshop
summary: Continual world models must decide whether new data justify changing the model. Fixed replay schedules and prediction-error triggers specify when to update, but neither reveals the value of an individual update: one deployment run cannot show how the same model would have performed at that moment had it held its parameters. We introduce the fork ledger, which branches a deployment stream at pre-registered decision points into matched update and hold continuations under common random numbers. It evaluates both continuations on the same episodes and records $ΔR = R_{\mathrm{update}} - R_{\mathrm{hold}}$. Always applying one fixed update mechanism lowers return on all three simulated control tasks: CartPole ($-144.0$; checkpoint-bootstrap $95\%$ CI $[-185.4,-116.1]$, against a converged return near $650$), Walker ($-82.8$; $[-101.1,-61.7]$) and Cheetah ($-18.6$; $[-29.0,-6.6]$). Divergence is an outcome of applying the update, so the estimand counts every attempted fork; restricted to the $693$ of $720$ that did not collapse, CartPole and Walker are unchanged in sign ($-113.4$ and $-82.1$) and Cheetah becomes unresolved ($-3.9$; $[-17.5,+13.0]$). The task is the unit of inference: each contributes $240$ attempted forks over five pretrained checkpoints crossed with two drift directions. The ledger makes counterfactual utility observable for a fixed mechanism, allowing triggers to be judged by the updates they select rather than by surprise detection alone.

AI.tldr: Researchers introduce the "fork ledger" method to evaluate continual world model updates by comparing counterfactual performance of update vs. hold decisions under common random numbers, revealing that automatic updates often harm performance.
AI.motivation: Current continual world models lack a way to measure the actual value of individual updates. Fixed replay schedules and prediction-error triggers don't reveal whether an update improves performance, as one deployment run can't show what would have happened if the model had kept its old parameters.
AI.method: The fork ledger creates matched continuations at decision points: one branch applies the update, the other holds the parameters, both evaluated on the same episodes under common random numbers. It records ΔR = R_update - R_hold. The method tests on three simulated control tasks (CartPole, Walker, Cheetah) with 240 attempted forks per task across five pretrained checkpoints and two drift directions.
AI.result: Always applying fixed updates lowered returns on all three tasks: CartPole (-144.0), Walker (-82.8), Cheetah (-18.6). When excluding the 27 of 720 forks that collapsed, CartPole and Walker remained negative (-113.4, -82.1) while Cheetah became statistically unresolved (-3.9). The ledger shows divergence is an outcome of applying updates, not just a detection problem.
AI.conclusion: The fork ledger makes counterfactual utility observable, allowing update mechanisms to be judged by the actual performance impact of the updates they select, rather than just by their ability to detect surprise. This reveals that automatic updates often harm performance even when they don't cause catastrophic collapse.

title: DRG-MAPPO: Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Air Combat
summary: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for complex decision-making in autonomous systems and air combat. While MARL has demonstrated significant potential in air combat, achieving sophisticated tactical coordination remains a non-trivial challenge. This difficulty is largely attributed to two primary limitations: (1) the absence of structured relational modeling hinders agents from capturing complex, time-varying interactions among battlefield entities; and (2) conventional flat architectures often lack the capability to explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in highly dynamic environments. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Dynamic Role-Graph Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (DRG-MAPPO), a novel MARL framework that integrates graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment. Specifically, DRG-MAPPO constructs a graph-based representation of battlefield interactions and leverages graph attention mechanisms to extract critical relational features among allies, enemies, and threats. Subsequently, a high-level policy employs a dynamic role assignment mechanism to determine tactical responsibilities (e.g., ``leader'' and ``supporter''). Conditioned on these roles and encoded graph-relational features, a low-level policy executes discrete maneuver actions, facilitating the joint optimization of tactical strategy and collaborative execution. Furthermore, a target-priority auxiliary task is designed to foster the emergence of behaviors such as focus-fire. Experimental results demonstrate that DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87%, suggesting that our framework effectively balances relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability for cooperative air combat.

AI.tldr: A novel hierarchical MARL framework called DRG-MAPPO integrates graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment to improve tactical coordination in cooperative air combat scenarios.
AI.motivation: Current MARL approaches in air combat face two main limitations: (1) lack of structured relational modeling prevents agents from capturing complex, time-varying battlefield interactions; and (2) conventional flat architectures fail to explicitly model tactical roles, leading to ambiguous task allocation in dynamic environments.
AI.method: DRG-MAPPO features a hierarchical architecture with graph-based relational modeling using attention mechanisms to capture interactions among allies, enemies, and threats. It includes a high-level policy for dynamic role assignment (e.g., "leader" and "supporter") and a low-level policy that executes maneuver actions based on roles and graph features. An auxiliary target-priority task promotes behaviors like focus-fire.
AI.result: Experimental results show DRG-MAPPO achieves a state-of-the-art win rate of 87%, outperforming existing methods and effectively balancing relational modeling, interpretability, and optimization stability in cooperative air combat scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DRG-MAPPO successfully addresses the limitations of conventional MARL approaches by combining graph-based relational modeling with dynamic role assignment, demonstrating superior tactical coordination and providing a framework that enhances both performance and interpretability in complex multi-agent decision-making tasks.

title: SemVerBench: Benchmarking LLM Comprehension of Version-Constraint Resolution Semantics
comment: Accepted at the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026). 8 pages, 6 tables
summary: Large language model (LLM) coding agents constantly decide whether a version satisfies a constraint such as ^1.2.3 or >=2.0,<3, yet their grasp of version-constraint semantics has never been measured directly. We introduce SemVerBench, the first benchmark of LLM version-constraint resolution semantics across three ecosystems (npm, PEP 440, Cargo): 240 machine-checkable items with unique answers, built author-neutrally from four balanced sources (each ecosystem's official test suite plus three frontier LLM proposers) and labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluating six frontier models, we find systematic, predictable per-mechanism blind spots: a partial-comparator carry rule (>1.2 means >=1.3.0) traps every model on Cargo (near 60%), and although standard PEP 440 prefix matching is universal, on zero-pad/post-release corner cases GPT-5.1 collapses (0/26) while Claude stays at 97-100% (verified on a 67-item oracle-validated set). Opus significantly outperforms all other models, and Sonnet outperforms the OpenAI models (McNemar). The failures look more like an activation/application gap than a knowledge gap: injecting the rule or a light correct hint recovers most errors, whereas interval decomposition does not, and models are at ceiling on the basic forms of the same rules. An author-stratified analysis finds no statistically significant self-favoritism. Because the task is verifiable and a free, 100%-correct resolver exists, tool delegation reaches ~100%: coding agents should delegate version resolution to a resolver rather than reason about versions in-head.

AI.tldr: SemVerBench is the first benchmark to measure LLMs' understanding of version-constraint semantics across three package ecosystems, revealing systematic blind spots that can be fixed by delegating to external resolvers rather than reasoning in-head.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents frequently need to evaluate version constraints (like "^1.2.3" or ">=2.0,<3") but their understanding of version-constraint semantics has never been directly measured or benchmarked.
AI.method: Created SemVerBench with 240 machine-checkable items across npm, PEP 440, and Cargo ecosystems using four balanced sources (official test suites + three frontier LLM proposers) and labeled by a non-circular two-implementation oracle. Evaluated six frontier models and analyzed error patterns, rule injection effects, and delegation strategies.
AI.result: Found systematic blind spots: all models trapped by Cargo's partial-comparator carry rule (~60% failure), GPT-5.1 collapsed on PEP 440 corner cases (0/26) while Claude maintained 97-100%. Opus significantly outperformed other models. Failures appear to be activation/application gaps rather than knowledge gaps - injecting rules recovered most errors. Tool delegation reached ~100% accuracy using existing resolvers.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents should delegate version resolution to dedicated external resolvers rather than attempt to reason about version constraints internally, as the task is verifiable and 100%-correct free resolvers exist for all major ecosystems.

title: Agentic Share-of-Search: A Multi-Agent AI System for Competitive Decision-Making in LLM-Mediated E-Commerce
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 Decision Science Institute Annual Conference
summary: AI shopping assistants increasingly redirect consumer discovery, creating an urgent need for tools that support seller-side competitive decision-making. We present a multi-agent AI system that automates competitive visibility measurement and root cause diagnosis in LLM-mediated ecommerce. The system introduces Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as the decision target, deploys query agents across leading AI platforms, and uses a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend prioritized merchandising interventions. A 100-trial ablation study, presented as a feasibility evaluation of this prototype, shows the agent recovers the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%, 5.5x over chance), rising to 63.9% among high-correlation ablations.

AI.tldr: AI system automates competitive visibility measurement in LLM-mediated ecommerce by deploying query agents across platforms and diagnosing root causes to recommend merchandising interventions.
AI.motivation: AI shopping assistants are increasingly redirecting consumer discovery, creating an urgent need for tools that support seller-side competitive decision-making in LLM-mediated ecommerce environments.
AI.method: Multi-agent AI system that: 1) introduces Agentic Share-of-Search (ASoS) as decision target, 2) deploys query agents across leading AI platforms, and 3) uses a ReAct-based diagnostic agent to recommend prioritized merchandising interventions.
AI.result: In a 100-trial ablation study (feasibility evaluation), the agent recovers the ablated signal in 39% of trials (95% CI: 30.0% - 48.8%, 5.5x over chance), rising to 63.9% among high-correlation ablations.
AI.conclusion: The system demonstrates feasibility for automating competitive visibility measurement and root cause diagnosis in AI-driven ecommerce, showing significant improvement over chance performance in recovering ablated signals.

title: An AI-Powered Culturally Aware Chatbot for Stress Detection and Wellness Support among Pakistani University Students Using NLP and Machine Learning
summary: With the existing digital mental health tools specifically developed for Western settings, Pakistani students are exposed to a uniquely compounded stress situation in their university that includes academic, financial, familial, and relational stressors, which have become a serious concern for academic and psychological development of students in Pakistani universities. This paper introduces a new, AI-driven and culturally sensitive stress detection and wellness support system that is tailored to the context of Pakistani university students. The system is based on a machine learning model called Random Forest which is trained using a validated student stress data set of 1100 responses on 20 features from psychological, physiological, academic, environmental and social aspects, with an accuracy of 89.09% and a macro F1-score of 0.89, in three stress severity levels. The classification outputs are passed on to an open-source large language model through OpenRouter API, where an appropriately crafted system prompt, culturally aware, gives the model a conversation about wellness, in English, Urdu and Roman Urdu. The second most predictive stress factor in this population identified by feature importance analysis was teacher-student relationship, which is a culturally important stress factor highlighting the need for region-aware mental health systems. Future research will involve primary data collection from students at various academic levels of Pakistani Universities with the validated DASS-21 instrument focusing on the students who are moving from FSc to undergraduate studies, which is a time of being psychologically vulnerable which is under-researched.

AI.tldr: Researchers developed an AI-driven, culturally sensitive stress detection system for Pakistani university students using Random Forest (89% accuracy) and LLM-based wellness support in English/Urdu.
AI.motivation: Existing digital mental health tools are developed for Western settings, but Pakistani students face unique compounded stressors (academic, financial, familial, relational) that seriously affect their academic and psychological development. There's a need for culturally sensitive mental health support systems tailored to this specific context.
AI.method: Created a machine learning system using Random Forest trained on 1100 responses with 20 features from psychological, physiological, academic, environmental, and social aspects. Classification outputs (three stress severity levels) are passed to an open-source LLM via OpenRouter API with culturally crafted system prompts for wellness conversations in English, Urdu, and Roman Urdu.
AI.result: The system achieved 89.09% accuracy and 0.89 macro F1-score for stress severity classification. Feature importance analysis identified teacher-student relationship as the second most predictive stress factor, highlighting the cultural importance of this relationship in Pakistani academic settings.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates the importance of culturally aware mental health systems and identifies specific cultural stress factors (like teacher-student relationships) unique to Pakistani students. Future work will involve primary data collection using DASS-21 instrument, focusing on the vulnerable transition period from FSc to undergraduate studies.

title: HERALD: High-Fidelity Exemplar Retrieval with Adaptive Landmark Distillation for Heterophily-Aware Graph Condensation
summary: Graph condensation aims to produce a small surrogate graph that preserves the downstream node-classification performance of a much larger original graph. Existing methods rely on Weisfeiler-Lehman neighbourhood aggregation or gradient-based distribution matching, both of which assume that adjacent nodes share the same label, an assumption that breaks down under heterophily. We propose HERALD (High-fidelity Exemplar Retrieval with Adaptive Landmark Distillation), a gradient-free graph condensation framework that adapts the node scoring and feature selection in the condensation pipeline to the graph's measured heterophily. HERALD selects features via a joint Fisher-discriminability and activation-density criterion that down-weights aggregated representations on heterophilic graphs, and scores nodes by a weighted combination of prototype representativeness, decision-boundary proximity, and Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID), where the weights are driven by a smooth sigmoid function of the heterophily ratio. Nodes are then assembled into a condensed subgraph through score-ordered BFS expansion, Personalised PageRank pruning, and class rebalancing, all at an identical storage budget to BONSAI, enabling direct comparison. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets spanning homophilic and heterophilic settings show that HERALD matches or outperforms state-of-the-art condensers on heterophilic graphs and remains competitive on homophilic ones across four GNN architectures.

AI.tldr: HERALD is a gradient-free graph condensation framework that adapts to graph heterophily using node scoring and feature selection, achieving state-of-the-art performance on heterophilic graphs while remaining competitive on homophilic ones.
AI.motivation: Existing graph condensation methods assume adjacent nodes share the same label (homophily), which breaks down in heterophilic graphs where connected nodes often have different labels. Current methods based on Weisfeiler-Lehman aggregation or gradient matching fail to handle heterophilic graphs effectively.
AI.method: HERALD uses a gradient-free approach with heterophily-adaptive techniques: 1) Feature selection via joint Fisher-discriminability and activation-density criterion that down-weights aggregated representations on heterophilic graphs; 2) Node scoring using weighted combination of prototype representativeness, decision-boundary proximity, and Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (LID), with weights controlled by a sigmoid function of heterophily ratio; 3) Graph assembly through score-ordered BFS expansion, Personalised PageRank pruning, and class rebalancing within identical storage budget to BONSAI.
AI.result: Experiments on eight benchmark datasets spanning homophilic and heterophilic settings show HERALD matches or outperforms state-of-the-art condensers on heterophilic graphs and remains competitive on homophilic ones across four GNN architectures.
AI.conclusion: HERALD successfully addresses the limitation of existing graph condensation methods on heterophilic graphs by introducing heterophily-adaptive feature selection and node scoring, providing a gradient-free framework that maintains performance across both homophilic and heterophilic graph types.

title: Off-Target Effects of Response-Style Alignment in a Korean 27B Language Model
comment: 19 pages. Korean-language evaluation (KoBBQ); all uncertainty estimates over KoBBQ items are clustered on the benchmark template
summary:
We post-train Qwen3.8-27B for Korean response style -- verbosity, list and markdown usage, discourse structure and register -- and measure two behaviours the objective never targets: abstention on ambiguous social questions in KoBBQ, where the benchmark-correct answer is UNKNOWN, and unprompted disclosure in securities guidance. Both move, and the changes are expressed primarily through the model's emission policy: how often it answers and how much it says.
  Matched target-form controls show that answer propensity depends on the training target, not the prompt set or recipe alone. Holding prompts, recipe, data volume and serving fixed and changing only the target text, three style seeds give positive answer-rate point estimates (mean +0.82 pp) and three neutral seeds negative ones (mean -1.53 pp); the observed seed ranges do not overlap and the means differ by 2.34 pp. A length-matched arm lies between them, and a fourth arm that stays short while preserving hedging is unstable across seeds, so which feature of the form is responsible is unresolved.
  For absolute stereotyped exposure the decomposition into an answer-propensity term and a conditional-composition term is an algebraic identity, not a finding; its empirical content is where the movement went. Across the trained checkpoints the changes are dominated by answer propensity while the composition term stays small, and because that term is evaluated on treatment-dependent answered subsets we do not read it as evidence about latent preference.
  Two measurement results follow. A between-arm contrast in conditional stereotyped share does not identify a change in conditional content preference when answer status is treatment-dependent. And agreement between two rule detectors for the same construct runs from 0.44 to 0.99 depending on which checkpoint produced the text -- observable without any reference labels.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that post-training large language models for Korean response style (verbosity, formatting, discourse structure) affects unintended behaviors like answer propensity on ambiguous questions and unprompted disclosure, primarily through changes in how often the model answers rather than content preferences.
AI.motivation: To understand how post-training for surface-level stylistic changes in Korean response style (verbosity, list/markdown usage, discourse structure, register) might affect unintended model behaviors, particularly abstention rates on ambiguous social questions and unprompted disclosure in securities guidance.
AI.method: Post-trained Qwen3.8-27B for Korean response style, then measured unintended behaviors on KoBBQ benchmark (ambiguous social questions where correct answer is UNKNOWN) and securities guidance. Used controlled experiments with matched target-form controls to isolate effects of training target from prompts/data. Conducted systematic variation of style seeds (positive, neutral, length-matched) while holding other factors constant.
AI.result: Style training affects answer propensity significantly: three positive style seeds increased answer rates by +0.82 pp on average, while three neutral seeds decreased by -1.53 pp. Changes are dominated by answer propensity (how often model answers) rather than conditional content preferences. The decomposition into answer-propensity and conditional-composition terms shows treatment-dependent measurement artifacts - rule detector agreement varies dramatically (0.44 to 0.99) depending on which checkpoint produced the text.
AI.conclusion: Stylistic post-training can unintentionally affect model behaviors like answer propensity, and these changes are expressed primarily through emission policy (answer frequency). Between-arm contrasts in conditional content share don't identify actual preference changes when answer status is treatment-dependent. Measurement results depend heavily on which model checkpoint produced the text, observable without reference labels.

title: REVA: Reusable Evidence View Aggregation for Context-Efficient RAG Serving
comment: Author's accepted manuscript. Accepted for publication in the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM)
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves knowledge-intensive large language model (LLM) applications by conditioning generation on retrieved documents, but longer contexts increase latency, key-value (KV) cache memory, and token cost. Post-retrieval compression can reduce this cost, yet existing compressors often operate independently for each query, rely on auxiliary models or rewriting, and introduce online overhead that can offset the benefit of shorter prompts. We revisit RAG compression from a data-mining perspective by aggregating historical query--document--model interactions into reusable evidence views. We first show that modern compressors have unstable gains over simple truncation and can add substantial inference-time latency. We then propose Reusable Evidence View Aggregation (REVA), a framework that mines the target generator's historical attention traces into a document-keyed, budget-agnostic score store. REVA maps token-level attention to readable word units, aggregates importance across repeated document accesses, and renders budget-specific plain-text views that preserve document order and the standard RAG interface. Across four representative benchmarks and modern LLMs, REVA improves generation quality by 1.0--5.8 points over existing advances, while reducing compression overhead by a factor of 5.3 to 15.6, adding less than 40 ms of latency.

AI.tldr: REVA is a framework that mines historical LLM attention patterns to create reusable compressed document views for RAG systems, reducing latency and costs while improving generation quality.
AI.motivation: Current RAG systems face latency, memory, and cost issues with long contexts. Existing compression methods have unstable performance, add inference-time overhead, and operate independently per query without leveraging historical data.
AI.method: REVA aggregates historical query-document-model interactions into evidence views by: 1) mining target generator's historical attention traces into document-keyed score stores, 2) mapping token-level attention to word units, 3) aggregating importance across repeated document accesses, and 4) generating budget-specific plain-text views preserving document order.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks and modern LLMs, REVA improves generation quality by 1.0-5.8 points over existing methods while reducing compression overhead by 5.3x to 15.6x and adding less than 40ms latency.
AI.conclusion: REVA demonstrates that data-mining approaches to RAG compression, by leveraging reusable historical evidence views, can significantly improve both efficiency and quality compared to query-independent or auxiliary model approaches.

title: Solving Few-Shot Multiobjective Multitask Optimization via Iterative Sequential Transfer
comment: Accepted paper in WCCI/CEC 2026
summary: Applying knowledge transfer across multiple optimization tasks, multitask optimization (MTO) emerges as a promising approach to solving synergistic optimization tasks simultaneously. However, the development of effective knowledge transfer mechanisms in MTO fundamentally relies on aligning elite solution distributions across tasks. This dependency creates a critical bottleneck in few-shot optimization regimes, as restricted evaluation budgets impede the identification of elite solution distributions required for beneficial transfer. This challenge is exacerbated in multiobjective multitask problems, where each optimizer must approximate a continuous Pareto manifold rather than a single optimal point. This paper introduces Iterative Sequential Transfer (IST) to circumvent this bottleneck. We model MTO as a sequence of sequential transfer optimization problems, concentrating evaluations on a single target per iteration. We propose a likelihood-informed task prioritization mechanism to maximize transfer utility by identifying the task most likely ready for knowledge integration. Empirical results on benchmark and real-world problems verify the effectiveness of the proposed method under tight budgets.

AI.tldr: IST introduces iterative sequential transfer for multitask optimization under tight evaluation budgets by focusing on one task per iteration and prioritizing tasks most ready for knowledge integration.
AI.motivation: Traditional multitask optimization (MTO) struggles in few-shot regimes where limited evaluation budgets prevent proper alignment of elite solution distributions needed for effective knowledge transfer. This is especially challenging in multiobjective problems where each task requires approximating a continuous Pareto manifold rather than a single optimal point.
AI.method: Proposes Iterative Sequential Transfer (IST) which models MTO as a sequence of sequential transfer optimization problems, concentrating evaluations on a single target task per iteration. Uses a likelihood-informed task prioritization mechanism to identify the task most likely ready for beneficial knowledge integration.
AI.result: Empirical results on benchmark and real-world problems demonstrate that IST effectively overcomes the knowledge transfer bottleneck and achieves superior performance under tight evaluation budgets compared to traditional MTO approaches.
AI.conclusion: IST provides a practical solution to the critical bottleneck in few-shot multitask optimization by strategically focusing computational resources and enabling effective knowledge transfer even when elite solution distributions cannot be accurately estimated.

title: MUtE: A Dual Framework for Concept Erasure and Counterfactual Interventions
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: Erasing concept-specific information from representations has been proven useful for mitigating bias or interpreting model decisions. The joint objective is to transform the original representations such that the target concept becomes unpredictable, while maximally preserving concept-unrelated information. In this work, we revisit the optimal bounds of concept erasure to derive a novel class of erasure functions that naturally induce a deterministic, dual counterfactual mapping. Bridging the gap between theoretical optimality and practical representation learning, we design an implementation that imposes a translational bias on counterfactual trajectories - a constraint that aligns with how many concepts geometrically manifest in modern language models. Our framework enables seamless navigation between concept erasure and counterfactual generation. We empirically demonstrate its efficacy in improving downstream algorithmic fairness and generating counterfactual texts.

AI.tldr: A novel concept erasure framework that achieves optimal bounds and enables deterministic counterfactual mapping, improving fairness and counterfactual generation in language models.
AI.motivation: Current concept erasure methods need to more effectively bridge theoretical optimality with practical representation learning, and better align with how concepts geometrically manifest in modern language models.
AI.method: Derived a new class of erasure functions from optimal bounds of concept erasure that induces deterministic dual counterfactual mapping, implemented with translational bias constraint on counterfactual trajectories matching concept geometry in language models.
AI.result: Empirically demonstrated efficacy in improving downstream algorithmic fairness and generating counterfactual texts, showing seamless navigation between concept erasure and counterfactual generation.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully bridges theory and practice for concept erasure, providing both optimal theoretical bounds and practical implementation that aligns with language model geometry, enabling improved fairness and interpretability.

title: Estimating Inconsistency Response Surfaces under Uncertainty in Cyber-Physical System Development
comment: Extended version of the paper accepted at IEEE ICDM 2026; 10 pages + appendix, 11 figures, 3 tables
summary: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) are commonly represented through multiple interconnected models. During development, CPS consistency requires that shared model elements remain compatible across these models. Uncertainty, for example, due to sensor noise or model abstraction, changes the admissible values of model elements and can introduce inconsistencies, i.e., situations in which models can no longer be jointly satisfied. While existing approaches can determine consistency for a given uncertainty configuration, they provide limited support for systematically exploring, analyzing, and explaining inconsistency across large uncertainty spaces. We address this challenge by reformulating inconsistency as an intervention response modeling problem. Using Saltelli sampling and multi-fidelity Monte Carlo estimation, we generate intervention-response datasets and train a surrogate model that directly predicts inconsistency from the propagated uncertainty geometry. Experiments on 48 scenarios and 10 CPS domains show that the surrogate matches Monte Carlo estimates while reducing evaluation time from milliseconds to microseconds, enabling orders-of-magnitude more response-surface evaluations within fixed computational budgets. Building on the learned response surfaces, we perform sensitivity analysis to identify dominant uncertainty drivers and introduce a gradient-based consistency recourse method to determine minimal uncertainty interventions that restore consistency. The results show that inconsistency under uncertainty can be effectively learned, analyzed, and repaired through response-surface modeling, providing a scalable foundation for uncertainty-aware consistency management in CPS development.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a response-surface modeling approach using surrogate models and sensitivity analysis to efficiently analyze and repair inconsistencies in Cyber-Physical Systems under uncertainty, reducing evaluation time from milliseconds to microseconds.
AI.motivation: Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) involve multiple interconnected models, and uncertainty (from sensor noise, model abstraction, etc.) can introduce inconsistencies where models can no longer be jointly satisfied. Existing approaches only determine consistency for given uncertainty configurations but lack systematic ways to explore, analyze, and explain inconsistency across large uncertainty spaces.
AI.method: The paper reformulates inconsistency as an intervention-response modeling problem. It uses Saltelli sampling and multi-fidelity Monte Carlo estimation to generate intervention-response datasets, then trains a surrogate model that predicts inconsistency from propagated uncertainty geometry. The approach enables sensitivity analysis to identify dominant uncertainty drivers and introduces a gradient-based consistency recourse method to determine minimal uncertainty interventions that restore consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on 48 scenarios across 10 CPS domains show the surrogate model matches Monte Carlo estimates while reducing evaluation time from milliseconds to microseconds, enabling orders-of-magnitude more response-surface evaluations within fixed computational budgets. The approach effectively learns, analyzes, and repairs inconsistency under uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Inconsistency under uncertainty in CPS can be effectively learned, analyzed, and repaired through response-surface modeling, providing a scalable foundation for uncertainty-aware consistency management in CPS development.

title: Combining Synthetic and Real Data for Low-Resource Historical OCR: A Manchu Case Study
summary: Manchu, now critically endangered, was one of the principal languages of the Qing empire (1636-1912), and its extensive archival record is increasingly digitized but remains difficult to search and analyze at scale. Previous work showed that vision-language models (VLMs) trained only on synthetic Manchu word images can reach 87.4% word accuracy on real Qing manuscripts and prints, leaving a substantial synthetic-to-real gap. This study examines how synthetic and real historical training data should be combined for low-resource OCR. Using 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images, we evaluate three pretrained VLMs and a compact convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN) under four regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training, following a common checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol. Introducing real training images raises the leading configurations to between 95.09% and 96.28% word accuracy, while no synthetic-only configuration exceeds 87.92%. Synthetic supplementation substantially improves all three VLMs, whereas its marginal effect for the CRNN is sensitive to the training objective. Joint and sequential training yield broadly similar archival accuracy under the tested practical pipelines. A compact CRNN also reaches the leading performance range once real images are available, showing that model scale alone does not determine recognition accuracy. Finally, complementary errors among strong recognizers allow voting to raise accuracy to 98.27% without additional training, while an eighteenth-century Manchu dictionary provides a principled rule for adjudicating disagreements.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models and CRNNs achieve high Manchu OCR accuracy (95-96%) by combining synthetic and real historical data, with voting ensemble reaching 98.27% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Manchu is critically endangered with extensive digitized archives, but existing OCR has substantial synthetic-to-real gap (87.4% accuracy). Need effective strategies to combine limited real historical data with synthetic data for low-resource OCR.
AI.method: Used 60,000 synthetic and 20,306 real historical word images. Evaluated three pretrained VLMs and one CRNN under four training regimes: synthetic-only, real-only, joint synthetic-real, and sequential synthetic-to-real training. Used checkpoint-selection and archival evaluation protocol.
AI.result: Real training images boosted accuracy to 95.09-96.28% (vs. ≤87.92% synthetic-only). Synthetic supplementation improved VLMs significantly. CRNN reached leading performance with real data. Voting ensemble achieved 98.27% accuracy using complementary errors, with dictionary-based adjudication rules.
AI.conclusion: Combining synthetic and real data is crucial for low-resource OCR. Joint/sequential training yield similar results. Model scale isn't primary factor - compact CRNN can match VLMs. Voting ensembles and dictionary rules effectively maximize accuracy without additional training.

title: Particle GFlowNets: Rethinking Generative Marginalization Models
comment: Accepted at UAI 2026
summary: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) have been recently introduced as efficient neural sampling models for any-order autoregressive modelling of discrete distributions. By learning both the marginal and conditional probabilities of a persistent-block Gibbs sampler, MaMs enable fast posterior evaluation with a single neural network forward pass. While prior work has considered MaMs to be distinct from Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets), a well-established paradigm for inference in discrete stochastic models, we show that they are equivalent. Then, we also extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes. In particular, we describe an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler, derived from the Gelman-Rubin statistic, which plays a key role in speeding up learning convergence. Our experiments show that our method, called Particle GFlowNets, markedly accelerates training in large combinatorial spaces.

AI.tldr: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) are shown to be equivalent to GFlowNets, and extended with non-autoregressive processes and automatic rejuvenation criterion using Gelman-Rubin statistic, creating Particle GFlowNets that accelerate training in combinatorial spaces.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to bridge the gap between two recent approaches for inference in discrete stochastic models: Generative Marginalization Models (MaMs) and Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets). While prior work considered them distinct, the authors seek to establish their equivalence and extend MaMs' capabilities with more efficient sampling strategies for large combinatorial spaces.
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate the equivalence between MaMs and GFlowNets. They then extend MaMs' sampling strategy to non-autoregressive generative processes by developing an automatic criterion for full-state rejuvenation of the Gibbs sampler based on the Gelman-Rubin statistic. This approach, named Particle GFlowNets, aims to speed up learning convergence.
AI.result: Experiments show that Particle GFlowNets markedly accelerate training in large combinatorial spaces compared to previous approaches, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed non-autoregressive extension and automatic rejuvenation criterion.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the equivalence between MaMs and GFlowNets, provides theoretical connections between these frameworks, and introduces Particle GFlowNets with improved sampling efficiency through non-autoregressive processes and automatic rejuvenation, offering faster convergence for inference in discrete stochastic models.

title: Characterizing Job Power Elasticity for Power-Flexible AI Training
summary:
Large language model (LLM) training is among the fastest-growing sources of electricity demand in modern data centers, and power availability is a primary bottleneck to continued AI infrastructure growth. Making the power consumption of these workloads flexible could unlock additional power for AI growth, limit increases in electricity prices, and improve the utilization of existing grid infrastructure. However, to realize this flexibility, we must first understand how the performance of training workloads changes when GPU power is reduced.
  This paper presents the first systematic characterization of \emph{job power elasticity} (the sensitivity of throughput to power reductions) in LLM training. To quantify elasticity, we introduce the \emph{Power Flexibility Index (PFI)}, a normalized metric that quantifies the performance cost of power reductions and provides a control primitive for SLA-aware power flexibility.
  We collect data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 (plus 24 H200 validation runs and 34 matched H100 runs), including both dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. We find that LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity, and we identify telemetry signals that predict PFI at runtime. Finally, we demonstrate that PFI-aware power allocation maximizes total tokens/second throughput under power constraints. Under a 30\% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, 63\% of the performance gap between an equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. Our results establish power elasticity as a measurable property of training jobs and provide a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure.

AI.tldr: LLM training has high electricity demand; making power consumption flexible could unlock AI growth. This paper introduces Power Flexibility Index (PFI) to measure job power elasticity and shows PFI-aware allocation maximizes throughput under power constraints.
AI.motivation: LLM training is rapidly increasing electricity demand in data centers, with power availability being a primary bottleneck for AI infrastructure growth. Making power consumption flexible could enable additional AI growth, limit electricity price increases, and improve grid infrastructure utilization. However, to achieve this flexibility, we need to understand how training performance changes when GPU power is reduced.
AI.method: The paper introduces the Power Flexibility Index (PFI) as a normalized metric to quantify job power elasticity (performance sensitivity to power reductions). Researchers collected data from 131 LLM training runs on H200 GPUs (plus validation runs on H200 and matched H100 runs), covering dense and mixture-of-experts models, pretraining and fine-tuning tasks, and up to 32 GPUs. They identify telemetry signals that predict PFI at runtime and demonstrate PFI-aware power allocation strategies.
AI.result: LLM training jobs exhibit substantial but variable power elasticity. Under a 30% power reduction, PFI-aware power allocation recovers ~1.5k tokens/s per job, achieving 63% of the performance gap between equal-weight allocation and an oracle with perfect information. The research shows that PFI-aware allocation maximizes total tokens/second throughput under power constraints.
AI.conclusion: Power elasticity is a measurable property of training jobs, and the Power Flexibility Index provides a foundation for power-aware, grid-responsive AI infrastructure. The findings enable SLA-aware power flexibility and demonstrate that intelligent power allocation can significantly recover performance under power constraints.

title: Enabling Knowledge Graph Understanding at Scale with the EXplore Your Graphs ENgine (EXYGEN)
summary: We present EXYGEN (EXplore Your Graphs ENgine), a framework for knowledge graph (KG) understanding that enables conversational access to KGs at scale. We address two questions in sequence. First, how effectively can LLMs perform text-to-SPARQL generation given only automatically derived structured metadata and small graph samples, rather than task-specific fine-tuning? We integrate VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline and ablate KG-derived context on the SciQA benchmark. Our best configuration -- combining ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs -- reaches an exact match of 0.419 on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. We further find that lexical metrics such as F1 poorly predict query correctness, and that larger general-purpose LLMs can outperform smaller code-specialized ones once given sufficient context. Second, we ask how to generate the structured metadata that this method relies on from very large KGs, where KG metadata generation becomes computationally intractable. We introduce a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy that preserves structural diversity while remaining computationally tractable. On OpenCitations Meta and GESIS, it retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x; on ORKG, sampling is not just faster but the only tractable path to obtain complete metadata. Together, these results show that structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs, though closing the remaining gap to fully fine-tuned approaches will likely require reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars -- whether through synthetic generation or an execution-feedback-driven approach -- and validating these findings beyond a single benchmark.

AI.tldr: EXYGEN framework enables scalable conversational access to knowledge graphs using LLMs with automatically derived metadata and efficient sampling strategies, reducing need for task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: To enable scalable conversational access to knowledge graphs by addressing two key challenges: 1) how effectively LLMs can perform text-to-SPARQL generation using only automatically derived structured metadata rather than fine-tuning, and 2) how to generate the required structured metadata from very large KGs where traditional approaches are computationally intractable.
AI.method: The framework uses a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline integrating VoID descriptions and ShEx schemas. It performs ablation studies on KG-derived context using SciQA benchmark. For large KGs, introduces a predicate-coverage-aware parallel graph sampling strategy that preserves structural diversity while remaining computationally tractable.
AI.result: Best configuration combining ShEx schemas, retrieved triples, and example question-query pairs achieves exact match of 0.419 on execution results without any LLM fine-tuning. On large KGs (OpenCitations Meta and GESIS), the sampling strategy retains high predicate coverage with minimal triple loss and reduces runtime by over 80x. For ORKG, sampling is the only tractable path to obtain complete metadata.
AI.conclusion: Structured schema context and lightweight prompting can substantially reduce reliance on fine-tuning for scalable conversational access to KGs, though closing the remaining gap to fully fine-tuned approaches will require reducing dependence on curated question-query exemplars through synthetic generation or execution-feedback-driven approaches, and validating findings beyond a single benchmark.

title: CoRA-NAS: Coarse Ranking and Anchor-Residual Refinement for Neural Architecture Search
summary: Zero-cost proxies rank architectures cheaply, but their reliability varies across search spaces. We introduce CoRA-NAS (COarse Ranking + Anchor-residual), a two-stage framework combining a static ranking prior with low-cost learning-curve refinement. CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies through an equal-weight log-rank consensus and a target-free consensus gate. CoRA-Refine samples anchors across this prior, extrapolates their early validation curves, and propagates a learned residual correction with an ExtraTrees model. The refinement uses approximately 1% of the cost of fully training the candidate set. Fully trained architecture-accuracy labels are not used to fit the ranker. One configuration is used across spaces, with space-specific architecture encodings. Across NAS-Bench-201, NAS-Bench-101, TransNAS-Bench-101, and NATS-SSS, CoRA-Refine achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894, respectively. Its worst-space correlation of 0.715 is the highest among the compared methods. On NAS-Bench-201/CIFAR-100, its selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy, near the reported ground-truth best of 73.37%. On the pure size space, refinement recovers the static prior's shortfall relative to parameter count, while remaining tied with the strongest capacity proxies within noise. The resulting framework combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection.

AI.tldr: CoRA-NAS: Two-stage NAS framework combining static zero-cost proxy ranking with cheap learning-curve refinement using only 1% cost, achieving strong cross-space ranking correlations.
AI.motivation: Zero-cost proxies for neural architecture search vary in reliability across different search spaces, requiring a robust method that works consistently well without expensive full training.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) CoRA-Rank aggregates capacity and structure-at-initialization proxies using equal-weight log-rank consensus and target-free consensus gate. 2) CoRA-Refine samples anchors, extrapolates early validation curves, propagates learned residual correction with ExtraTrees model using only ~1% training cost.
AI.result: Achieves mean Spearman correlations of 0.946, 0.715, 0.786, and 0.894 across four NAS benchmarks. Selected architecture reaches 73.32% accuracy (near ground-truth best 73.37%). Worst-space correlation of 0.715 outperforms compared methods.
AI.conclusion: CoRA-NAS combines cross-space ranking robustness with low-cost architecture selection, effectively addressing zero-cost proxy reliability issues without requiring expensive full training.

title: SIRF: A Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model for Industrial Content Risk Control
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the Industry Track of EMNLP 2026
summary: For industrial content risk control, the real deployment constraint is not average accuracy but how much risk can be auto-handled under high precision and second-level latency. We present SIRF (Spec-Internalized Risk Foundation Model), which internalizes a platform's complex policies, synthesized without additional human annotation via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting and account-level chain-of-thought (CoT), into the weights via continued pretraining (CPT), so rules are applied at high precision under an ultra-low-latency, verdict-only deployment. A controlled same-source comparison (Qwen3-8B-SFT vs. SIRF-8B-SFT, identical policy injection and verdict-only output form, differing only in policy-grounded CPT) attributes the gain to internalization: SIRF-8B-SFT reaches 71.3% Black Recall@P95, +15.1pp over the baseline, using only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general ability, and among included, logprob-available models under this interface it matches or exceeds far larger systems. SIRF is deployed as a tree-model adjudication layer (20% more mis-penalized samples recovered) and transfers to a freezing scenario at low cost (~70% relative mis-penalization reduction).

AI.tldr: SIRF internalizes platform policies via continued pretraining to auto-handle content risks with high precision and ultra-low latency, achieving 71.3% Black Recall@P95 with only ~70M tokens.
AI.motivation: Industrial content risk control requires high precision and second-level latency, not just average accuracy, to automatically handle risks under real deployment constraints.
AI.method: Internalizes complex policies via EntiGraph, MAGA rewriting, and account-level chain-of-thought into model weights through continued pretraining, enabling verdict-only deployment with ultra-low latency.
AI.result: SIRF-8B-SFT achieves 71.3% Black Recall@P95 (+15.1pp over baseline) with only ~70M CPT tokens without harming general abilities, matching or exceeding larger systems.
AI.conclusion: SIRF enables effective content risk control deployment as tree-model adjudication layer with 20% recovery of mis-penalized samples and transfers well to freezing scenarios with ~70% relative mis-penalization reduction.

title: General Quantification of Covariate and Concept Shifts
comment: 38 pages, 9 figures, accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Generalization under distribution shift remains a core challenge in modern machine learning, yet existing learning bound theory is limited to narrow, idealized settings and is non-estimable from samples. In this paper, we bridge the gap between theory and practical applications. We first show that existing definition of concept shift breaks when the source and target supports mismatch. Leveraging entropic optimal transport, we propose a key notion: $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, and derive a general error bound unifying covariate and $γ^{*}\!$-concept shifts, which applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling. We further develop estimators for these shifts with concentration guarantees, and the DataShifts algorithm, which can quantify distribution shifts and estimate the error bound in most applications - a rigorous and general tool for analyzing learning error under distribution shift.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new framework for analyzing generalization under distribution shift using entropic optimal transport, proposes measurable shift estimators, and develops a practical algorithm for quantifying shifts and estimating error bounds.
AI.motivation: Existing generalization theory for distribution shifts is limited to narrow, idealized settings and cannot be estimated from samples, creating a gap between theory and practical applications in modern machine learning.
AI.method: Uses entropic optimal transport to define γ*-concept shifts that handle source-target support mismatches, derives general error bounds unifying covariate and concept shifts, develops shift estimators with concentration guarantees, and creates the DataShifts algorithm.
AI.result: Developed a rigorous framework for analyzing learning error under distribution shift that applies to broad loss functions, label spaces, and stochastic labeling, with practical estimators and algorithm for most applications.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework bridges theory and practice for distribution shift analysis, providing a general, estimable tool for quantifying shifts and error bounds in real-world applications.

title: MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
comment: Preprint version
summary: Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology: continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo contains 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types with controllable difficulty. We benchmark 14 MLLMs and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, including 3 video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning, and the best-performing model remains far below observed human performance. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach plausible endpoints, but audited rollouts do not reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions. Our website is at https://mind-topo.github.io/

AI.tldr: MindTopo is a new benchmark for evaluating foundation models' understanding of topological relations (continuity, separation, order, enclosure, knots) at two cognitive levels: reasoning and planning, showing current models perform poorly compared to humans.
AI.motivation: Current foundation model evaluations focus mainly on metric or viewpoint-dependent spatial relations, but cognitive science shows topological relations (invariant under continuous deformation) are foundational to spatial understanding.
AI.method: Created MindTopo benchmark with 11,030 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types testing 5 topological properties. Evaluated 14 MLLMs and studied agent configurations with image/video generation, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning experiments.
AI.result: All MLLMs performed better on reasoning than planning, with best models far below human performance. Generated observations retained local cues but rollout trajectories didn't reliably follow environment dynamics or preserve topology across transitions.
